lesson_title: Grip, Ramps and the Push That Isn't the Weight
hook_text: A wardrobe ignores your first shove, ignores your second — then suddenly gives. That lurch is two frictions swapping shifts.
clip_script: Shove a wardrobe: nothing. Harder: nothing. One more heave — and it lurches loose, then slides easily. Here is what happened. While it stood still, friction was MATCHING you, newton for newton. Shove 250, it resists 250. But matching has a ceiling: the grip coefficient times the floor's push. Beat the ceiling and a weaker friction takes over — that is the lurch, and that is why starting is harder than keeping going. Now tilt the world. On a ramp, gravity splits into two shares: one pulling downhill, weight times sine, and one pressing into the surface, weight times cosine. The surface only answers the pressing share — so on a slope the grip is built on a SMALLER push. Steeper hill, weaker grip. And the best trick in the topic: to know if something slides, you do not need its mass at all. Compare the tangent of the angle with the grip coefficient. Tangent 35 degrees is 0,700; coefficient 0,6 — it slides. Fifteen kilograms or one hundred and fifty: same answer.
visual_style: A stubborn wardrobe with a growing force bar that snaps at the ceiling value; then a ramp tilting up while a weight arrow splits into two glowing shares and the grip bar shrinks; a tangent-versus-mu scoreboard for the finale.
mood: Physical and satisfying — furniture-moving frustration decoded into two clean rules.
pacing: Slow tease on the stuck wardrobe, snap release, brisk ramp tilt, punchline on the mass-free test.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never write N equals mg on a slope again.
